title: Research Bite #4: Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #4 covers Chunliang Yang, Liang Luo, and colleagues' Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis “Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning,” a systematic review pooling 573 effect sizes from 222 studies and nearly 48,500 students. The headline finding is a large average effect size of 0.499 — students who are tested on material perform about half a standard deviation higher than those who are not — which the authors note exceeds the average effect size found across more than 800 meta-analyses of educational interventions generally. The benefit holds regardless of subject area, educational level, or quiz format, is strengthened by corrective feedback after quizzing, and is larger for post-instruction quizzes than pre-instruction ones. Crucially, the review counters the “drill and kill” critique of testing directly: quizzing improves conceptual understanding and problem-solving, not just rote recall of facts. Barton's takeaway is that in-class time spent quizzing is not time stolen from teaching — it is itself one of the most reliably effective teaching moves available, especially when matched in format to the eventual assessment and paired with feedback.
points: An average effect size of 0.499 across 573 effect sizes and nearly 48,500 students is, by educational-intervention standards, a large effect — bigger than the average found across more than 800 meta-analyses of educational interventions generally.

The testing effect held regardless of subject area or educational level (elementary through university), which undercuts the common objection that quizzing only helps in certain subjects or age groups.

Matching quiz format to eventual exam format produced larger learning gains than mismatched formats — direct support for retrieval-practice theory that the act of recalling information from memory, not just re-exposure to it, is what drives the benefit.
The review explicitly counters the “drill and kill” criticism of testing: quizzing improved conceptual learning and problem-solving skills, not only factual recall.

Corrective feedback after quizzes further increased learning outcomes, and low-stakes quizzes were found to have minimal effect on — and could even reduce — test anxiety, addressing a common teacher concern about frequent testing.
quotes: This paper from the Psychological Bulletin is a systematic review of the effects of testing on classroom learning. The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 573 effect sizes from 222 studies, which included data from nearly 48,500 students.

Testing or quizzing in the classroom is an effective learning tool and can raise students’ academic achievement by about half a standard deviation. This effect is larger than the average effect size found in over 800 meta-analyses on educational interventions.

Frequent testing is more beneficial than infrequent testing, and the more class content is quizzed, the greater the student learning gains. Teachers should offer corrective feedback after quizzes to further increase student learning outcomes.

Quizzing does not only improve factual learning, but also conceptual learning and problem-solving skills. This evidence counters the argument that testing is a ‘drill and kill’ strategy and only promotes memorization.
Matching quiz and exam formats yield larger learning gains than mismatched formats, supporting the idea that retrieving information from memory is helpful for learning.
Overall, testing is not only an assessment of learning but also an assessment for learning
